chapter: Jam sessions, pay and the Vanguard (retyped)
title: Big Bill Broonzy and Wild Bill at the Vanguard
summary: Hodes recalls Big Bill Broonzy grabbing a whiskey bottle and mentions Broonzy's protest songs. He thinks Broonzy was underestimated as a guitarist.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Billie Holiday as the musicians knew her

blocks.x: He worked also as an act, and that's where Big Bill -- I always remember, Big Bill Broonzy and Wild Bill Davison and going out and getting a fifth of booze, of some kind of whiskey. And Wild Bill had a drink and then Big Bill grabbed the bottle. And when he got through putting it down behind -- from his mouth, I could see where the bottom of his fist was, the whiskey was below that bottom. And I says, no more, I ain't going in with him in no bottles no more.

But he was a real warm character, and he was a great player. I think he was so underestimated, but if you happened to hear the recording of him playing by himself on guitar and see what he could do with a guitar and how many tunes he wrote, just the most obvious, When You're White You're All Right, When You're Brown Stick Around, and When You're
Black Get In The Back, way back, things like that. But that was a protest. But he wrote blues, too. I forget all of them. But he was really something to work for.
So all this was happening at the Vanguard. Next was down the block and across the street. The Village was jumping.
